title: Book 02 — Chapter 8, Part 1: Revised Exam Questions and Model Answers

source.title: Chapter 8, Part 1: The Universal Justice
source.author: Ayatullah Murtadha Mutahhari
source.method: Each question and model answer was checked against the original Al-Islam.org chapter. Philosophical positions are presented as Mutahhari describes them; his response to the longevity objection is distinguished from empirical scientific proof.

revision_policy: Exam-ready model answers, not answer fragments.
Keep the four theories of justice distinct and explain Mutahhari’s criticism of each.
Attribute historical, philosophical, and hadith material to the source.
Do not import Chapter 8 Part 2’s discussion of political claimants or its reform-versus-corruption argument.

questions.prompt: What are the two essential purposes of the prophets’ mission according to Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari identifies two essential purposes. The first is to establish the proper relationship between the human being and the Creator: humanity must worship God rather than created things. This is summarized by tawhid, or the declaration that there is no god but Allah. The second is to establish just and righteous relations among human beings, including justice, peace, purity, cooperation, benevolence, affection, and service. The first mission concerns the relationship between humanity and God; the second concerns relationships within human society. Mutahhari stresses that social justice is not an optional addition to religion but one of the central purposes for which the prophets were sent.

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari mean by universal justice, and how is it different from individual or relative justice?
questions.answer: Universal justice refers to a future condition of human society in which oppression is no longer built into social life. Mutahhari describes it as the disappearance of tyranny, discrimination, war, hatred, bloodshed, exploitation, and the methods that sustain them, such as lying, hypocrisy, and deception. It is broader than one person receiving fair treatment in a particular dispute. It concerns the transformation of society as a whole so that justice, peace, purity, and genuine human relations become dominant. Mutahhari is therefore discussing a universal social order, not merely personal fairness or the correction of isolated wrongs.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari reject the view that justice belongs only to the next world?
questions.answer: Mutahhari challenges the pessimistic view that oppression is permanent in earthly life and that justice can occur only in the Hereafter. He argues that the Qur’an gives glad tidings about the future of humanity in this world: the faithful who do righteous deeds will inherit the earth, their religion will be established, and fear will be replaced by security. The age of war, moral corruption, and darkness is temporary; the final direction of human history is toward justice and luminosity. This does not deny the Hereafter or the reality of present oppression. It means that divine justice also has a promised historical and social manifestation in this world.

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari use Qur’an 57:25 to show that establishing justice is part of the prophets’ mission?
questions.answer: Mutahhari points to Qur’an 57:25, which states that God sent messengers with clear proofs and sent down the Scripture and the Balance so that people may maintain justice. He interprets the Book as revelation and the Balance as the just rules, standards, and regulations needed for human society. The verse therefore connects the sending of prophets and revealed guidance directly with the establishment of justice among people. Mutahhari concludes that justice is not merely a private virtue or a later political concern; it is a general purpose of prophetic missions. He uses this Qur’anic evidence to ground his discussion of universal justice.

questions.prompt: Define justice according to Mutahhari. What is its relationship to oppression and discrimination?
questions.answer: Mutahhari defines justice as giving each person the right or entitlement that is due to them in light of their creation, qualifications, talents, and activities. It is the opposite of oppression because oppression deprives a person of what they are entitled to receive. It is also the opposite of discrimination: when two people are in equal relevant circumstances, one must not be granted a privilege that is unfairly withheld from the other. Justice is therefore not simply whatever a powerful person or legal authority declares. It is grounded in real entitlement and the recognition of what is due to each person.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari say that justice does not always mean giving everyone identical treatment?
questions.answer: Mutahhari distinguishes equal treatment from mechanically identical treatment. Justice requires that people who are equal in the relevant respect should not be treated differently through arbitrary privilege or discrimination. However, people may differ in their qualifications, abilities, contributions, needs, or activities, and these relevant differences can affect what each person is entitled to receive. Therefore, giving everyone exactly the same thing in every circumstance is not necessarily just. The central question is whether a difference in treatment is supported by a genuine difference in entitlement, rather than favoritism or oppression. Equality is important, but it must be understood through the rights and qualifications of the people concerned.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari argue that justice is real rather than merely a command imposed by the powerful?
questions.answer: Mutahhari rejects the claim that justice is nothing more than force or whatever the law declares. He argues that justice is meaningful because entitlement is real. Creation gives beings particular qualities and capacities, and human actions and activities can establish further qualifications and rights. If a person has a genuine entitlement, then giving that person what is due has an objective meaning. Justice can therefore be defined as giving the right to its rightful owner. Mutahhari’s reasoning is that justice is rooted in the reality of creation and entitlement, not simply in the preferences of rulers or the strength of those who make laws.

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari mean by saying that the desire for justice may be part of human nature?
questions.answer: Mutahhari asks whether people can desire justice for its own sake, even when it brings them no immediate personal benefit. He compares this possibility with the natural appreciation of beauty: a person can enjoy beauty without being forced by law or promised a reward. In the same way, he asks whether a human being can love justice as an ideal and wish for a just society even when personal advantage is not at stake. The issue is not merely whether people sometimes obey rules, but whether they can develop an inner disposition that values justice itself. This question prepares the discussion of competing philosophical explanations and the Islamic view.

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari describe the position associated with Nietzsche and Machiavelli on justice?
questions.answer: Mutahhari presents Nietzsche and Machiavelli as representatives of a view that rejects justice as an independent ideal rooted in human nature. In the account he gives, justice is treated as an idea invented by the weak because they lack the power to defend themselves against the strong. If those who speak about justice acquired power, this theory assumes that they would behave like other powerful people. The practical advice associated with this position is to pursue power rather than justice. Mutahhari uses Nietzsche’s image of people speaking of justice because they lack the strength or “claws” to dominate others to illustrate this outlook.

questions.prompt: What is Bertrand Russell’s view of justice as presented by Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains Russell’s position as an argument that people should pursue justice because their own interests ultimately depend on justice being established for everyone. Even if a person is naturally self-interested, knowledge and rational calculation can show that harming others invites retaliation and reduces one’s own welfare. Therefore, an individual should recognize that personal benefit is connected to the public interest. On this view, justice is not necessarily loved for its own sake; it is supported because enlightened self-interest shows that a just society benefits each individual.

questions.prompt: What weakness does Mutahhari identify in the argument that people will be just because justice serves their own interests?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that this theory works only while a person fears retaliation from someone more powerful. A weak person may behave justly because a stronger neighbour can punish wrongdoing. But if that person gains overwhelming power and becomes confident that nobody can retaliate, the calculation of self-interest may no longer lead to justice. The powerful person may then oppress others without fearing a cost. Mutahhari concludes that enlightened self-interest does not provide a sufficient foundation for universal justice, because it cannot guarantee justice when power is unequal and the powerful face no effective threat of retaliation.

questions.prompt: What is the Marxist explanation of how justice will be established, as described by Mutahhari?
questions.answer: Mutahhari describes the Marxist view as one in which justice will arise automatically from changes in economic and productive systems rather than from moral transformation in individuals. In this account, economic development moves society from capitalism toward socialism, and socialism is expected to produce justice whether people personally desire it or not. Individuals are not considered the decisive agents of justice; changes in the economic structure are expected to bring it about. Mutahhari presents this as a theory that places confidence in the automatic operation of material and economic forces rather than in the cultivation of justice-seeking human beings.

questions.prompt: What is the central claim of the Islamic view of justice presented by Mutahhari?
questions.answer: The Islamic view, as Mutahhari presents it, rejects pessimism about human nature. It holds that the desire for justice genuinely exists within human beings, although it may not yet have reached its full development. Through proper training and guidance, a person can mature to the point of loving justice as one loves beauty and preferring public justice to personal advantage. Justice is therefore not merely imposed by force, produced by calculations of self-interest, or generated automatically by economic machinery. It can become an inward moral ideal through the perfection and education of the human being.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari present Imam ‘Ali as evidence against theories that deny genuine justice-seeking in human nature?
questions.answer: Mutahhari presents Imam ‘Ali as an example of a person who loved and upheld justice even when doing so did not serve his personal interests. Such a person cannot be explained simply by fear of retaliation, a calculation of material advantage, or automatic economic change. Imam ‘Ali demonstrates that a human being can make justice an inner ideal and sacrifice personal benefit for it. Mutahhari also says that ‘Ali should not be dismissed as an impossible exception: people raised by him and other genuinely pious individuals show that this disposition can exist in human beings. The example supports the Islamic claim that moral training can produce sincere justice-seeking.

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari correct the idea that the reappearance of Imam al-Mahdi would return humanity to the Age of Ignorance?
questions.answer: Mutahhari says that the reappearance should be understood in the opposite way: as an intellectual, moral, and scientific advancement of humanity. The promised age is not a regression to ignorance or a collapse of human development. It is a stage in which human beings become more mature, their wisdom increases, and their conduct becomes more just. He cites traditions in Usul al-Kafi describing the enhancement of people’s intellect and deeds. Thus, the age of the Imam is presented as the completion and elevation of human capacities, not a return to an earlier and less developed condition.

questions.prompt: What does Mutahhari cite from Usul al-Kafi about the condition of human beings when Imam al-Mahdi reappears?
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites a report in Usul al-Kafi stating that when the Imam of the Time reappears, God will enhance people’s wisdom, intellect, and deeds. He explains the image that there will no longer be a wolf-and-sheep relationship in the world: even the “wolves” will live in peace. He clarifies that the reference is not simply to animals but to human beings with predatory or oppressive natures. The report therefore depicts the promised age as a transformation of human character, in which people’s moral and intellectual development makes peaceful relations possible.

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari respond to the objection that the long life of Imam al-Mahdi is impossible under natural law?
questions.answer: Mutahhari challenges the assumption that the limits currently recognized by human science exhaust the possibilities of nature. He points to unresolved questions about the origin of the first living organism and the stages through which life emerged, arguing that science has not explained every major transition in the history of life. He also notes that scientific knowledge of biological limits may change and that future discoveries could extend human lifespan. He compares extraordinary longevity with other events that exceed ordinary experience, including revelation. His argument is a philosophical response to a claim of impossibility, not an empirical scientific demonstration of the Imam’s lifespan.

questions.prompt: Compare the four approaches to justice discussed by Mutahhari: Nietzsche and Machiavelli, Bertrand Russell, the Marxist view, and the Islamic view.
questions.answer: Mutahhari examines four explanations of how justice can or should be established. First, the position associated with Nietzsche and Machiavelli treats justice as an invention of the weak and advises people to pursue power instead. Second, Bertrand Russell’s view, as Mutahhari presents it, supports justice because rational self-interest shows that the individual benefits when society is just. Third, the Marxist view expects justice to arise automatically from changes in economic and productive systems, particularly the transition from capitalism to socialism, without requiring individuals to become justice-seeking. Fourth, the Islamic view holds that justice is rooted in human nature and can be brought to maturity through moral education and guidance. Mutahhari criticizes the first three as inadequate: power cannot provide justice, self-interest may fail when the powerful fear no retaliation, and economic machinery cannot replace moral agency. He prefers the Islamic view because it recognizes the possibility of people who love justice for its own sake, as exemplified by Imam ‘Ali and other righteous individuals.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari consider the Islamic view of justice stronger than explanations based only on force, self-interest, or economic change?
questions.answer: Mutahhari considers the Islamic view stronger because it takes seriously the possibility of genuine moral transformation. A theory based on force cannot guarantee justice when the powerful are no longer afraid of retaliation. A theory based on self-interest may persuade people to act justly only when justice protects their own welfare. A theory based on economic change leaves justice to automatic material processes and does not explain why individuals should become sincerely just. The Islamic view, by contrast, maintains that the desire for justice exists within human nature and can be developed through proper training and guidance. Justice can become an inner ideal, valued even when it conflicts with personal advantage. Mutahhari points to Imam ‘Ali and other righteous people as historical examples showing that such justice-seeking is possible. The argument is that the human being can be morally perfected, not merely restrained or managed.

questions.prompt: Set out Mutahhari’s argument about the possibility of Imam al-Mahdi’s long life. What does the argument establish, and what does it not establish?
questions.answer: Mutahhari begins with the objection that a human being cannot live for an extraordinarily long period because this would violate natural law. He responds that people often confuse the limits of current scientific knowledge with the limits of nature itself. He points to unresolved questions about the origin of the first living organism and the emergence of life, and argues that science has not explained every major transition in the history of living beings. He also observes that biological knowledge may develop and that future discoveries could extend human lifespan. He compares the possibility of extraordinary longevity with revelation and other events that exceed ordinary experience. The argument establishes, in Mutahhari’s reasoning, that long life should not be declared impossible merely because it is unusual or not explained by current knowledge. It does not provide empirical measurement or a scientific proof of the Imam’s lifespan; it challenges the claim of impossibility by appealing to the limits of human knowledge and divine power.

questions.prompt: Describe the characteristics of Imam al-Mahdi’s age that Mutahhari presents through the Prophetic traditions.
questions.answer: Mutahhari cites traditions describing the age of Imam al-Mahdi as one in which oppression is replaced by justice and fear by security. Wealth will be distributed fairly, and people’s hearts will be filled with spiritual richness rather than merely material abundance. Poverty, need, misery, hatred, and jealousy will disappear. The earth will disclose its resources and blessings, and people will be able to travel safely; one report describes even a weak elderly woman travelling from the east to the west without difficulty. Mutahhari also cites traditions about the restoration of justice and the revival of the Qur’an and Sunnah. These descriptions show that the promised age is not limited to a change in political leadership. It involves economic fairness, public safety, moral purification, spiritual abundance, and the restoration of divine guidance.

questions.prompt: Explain the significance of Imam ‘Ali’s description of war in Nahj al-Balaghah, Sermon 138, within Mutahhari’s discussion of the age before the Mahdi’s reappearance.
questions.answer: Mutahhari quotes Imam ‘Ali’s description of war as a force that appears attractive to those who initiate it but has a bitter outcome. The image of war displaying its teeth and offering milk suggests that its instigators may believe it will bring advantage, power, or benefit. Imam ‘Ali’s warning is that the apparent gains are deceptive and the final consequences are destructive. Mutahhari applies this warning to the dangerous conflicts and upheavals that can precede the promised transformation. He then connects the passage with the prediction that a divinely guided ruler will hold former rulers and officials accountable, restore just conduct, and revive the Qur’an and Sunnah. The point is that justice requires more than military victory: it requires accountability, moral restoration, and a different basis for governing society.

questions.prompt: Why is Imam al-Mahdi called al-Qa’im, and how does Mutahhari connect this title with the establishment of justice?
questions.answer: Mutahhari explains that al-Qa’im is a title derived from the idea of rising or standing forth. Whereas the other Imams are associated with titles reflecting particular qualities, the Imam of the Time is especially identified with rising to establish justice. Mutahhari connects the title with reports that he will rule justly, end cruelty and oppression, restore the Qur’an and Sunnah, and establish security throughout the world. The title therefore expresses the active and public character of the Imam’s mission. It is not merely a name; it summarizes the promised uprising through which oppression will be replaced by a just order. Mutahhari’s discussion links the title to the practical results of justice: safe roads, fair distribution, public security, and the disappearance of poverty.

questions.prompt: How does Mutahhari respond to modern pessimism about humanity’s future, especially in light of destructive scientific and military power?
questions.answer: Mutahhari acknowledges that modern science and technology have given humanity destructive powers on an unprecedented scale. He refers to fears expressed by Bertrand Russell and Einstein that scientific development could bring about humanity’s destruction, and he notes that a world war could leave no true victor because the human race and the earth would be the main losers. However, he rejects the conclusion that humanity’s future is therefore hopeless. He argues that Islamic belief, grounded in Qur’anic promises, teaches that oppression and darkness are temporary and that the final outcome will be justice and security. The promise of divine assistance and the future establishment of justice gives believers grounds for optimism even when human capabilities are being used destructively. His point is not that technological dangers are unreal, but that they do not determine the final destiny of humanity.

questions.prompt: Why does Mutahhari say that the universal justice of the Mahdi’s age will be rooted in spiritual and moral maturity rather than merely in enlightened self-interest?
questions.answer: Mutahhari argues that the justice of the promised age will go beyond people calculating that their own interests are protected when others are treated fairly. In the final just society, the human spirit will have been elevated and moral training will have reached completion. Justice will be valued as an intrinsic good and will be grounded in faith, worship of God, and knowledge of God. This means that people will not act justly merely because they fear retaliation or expect a personal advantage. Their inner character will have developed so that justice itself becomes a deeply held ideal. Mutahhari therefore connects universal justice with the completion of human spiritual development and with a government based on the Qur’an. The transformation is both social and inward: society becomes just because human beings themselves have matured.

questions.prompt: Which two thinkers does Mutahhari associate with the view that people should pursue power rather than justice?
questions.answer: Nietzsche and Machiavelli

questions.prompt: Which thinker’s view does Mutahhari describe as grounding justice in the individual’s enlightened self-interest?
questions.answer: Bertrand Russell

questions.prompt: Which source does Mutahhari cite for the report that people’s intellect and deeds will increase when the Imam of the Time reappears?
questions.answer: Usul al-Kafi

questions.prompt: Qur’an 57:25 says that the Book and the Balance were sent down so that mankind may maintain ______.
questions.answer: justice

questions.prompt: Mutahhari cites Imam ‘Ali’s description of war from Nahj al-Balaghah, Sermon ______.
